main.tex: 79: One way to address this challenge is to combine an observed label with evidence from nearby training nodes. When their labels provide consistent evidence for the underlying class, aggregating them can reduce the influence of isolated annotation errors. Related methods use neighborhood consistency to identify potentially mislabeled samples or encourage agreement between neighboring predictions \cite{ref10,ref11}. For graph data, a graph contrastive representation learned from node attributes and connectivity without class labels provides a basis for identifying such local groups \cite{ref12}. The remaining challenge is to form local regions from the representation geometry before aggregating labels, so that annotation errors do not determine which nodes contribute evidence.

81: Granular ball computing offers one way to construct such regions. It groups samples into coarse-grained units summarized by their centers and radii \cite{ref13}. Subsequent studies have investigated granular ball sampling for noisy or imbalanced classification \cite{ref15} and refined adaptive ball generation \cite{ref16}. Unlike supervised granular ball classifiers that use label purity to guide splitting, GB-LCSS forms balls from representation geometry under size and ball-count constraints before aggregating training labels.

103: Methods for learning with noisy labels reduce the influence of corrupted annotations by selecting training samples, encouraging consistent predictions, or modifying the training objective. Sample-selection methods use the training loss to assess label reliability: Co-teaching \cite{ref17} exchanged small-loss samples between two networks, and JoCoR \cite{ref18} additionally encouraged prediction agreement. Local relationships offer another source of evidence. Deep k-NN \cite{ref11} filtered out samples whose labels disagreed with those of their neighbors, while neighbor-consistency regularization \cite{ref10} encouraged the prediction for each sample to match those of its neighbors. Affinity-aware uncertainty quantification (AUQ) \cite{pr2026auq} instead examined sample--prototype relationships to quantify uncertainty and refine pseudo-labels.
157: GB-LCSS first learns a label-free graph representation and then uses its geometry to partition the nodes into granular balls.
185: The mean radius is the average Euclidean distance from the member representations to the ball center. A smaller value indicates a more compact ball.

537: The usefulness of local evidence depends on both its class composition and the number of available votes. Proposition~\ref{prop:local_vote} relates these quantities to voting reliability under independent symmetric noise. Agreement alone is insufficient when the local labels favor an incorrect class, since the consensus can then move the target away from the true class. The representation and parameter studies show lower accuracy when local groups fail to form or voting support becomes sparse. Under uniform 0.4 noise, CoraFull has both the lowest proportion of training nodes with a positive clean-vote margin (36.13\%) and the smallest net reduction in target Brier score among the five datasets (Appendix~I.2). With clean training labels, refinement raises mean accuracy on one dataset and lowers it on four, with all changes within 2.00 percentage points (Appendix~D). These results indicate that the benefit varies across datasets and supervision conditions.

highlights.text: Granular ball local consensus for graph-free node classification under label noise
Construct granular balls from graph contrastive representations without labels.
Transfer training graph structure into soft targets for attribute-only prediction.
Refine noisy supervision using leave-one-out consensus within granular balls.
Achieve the highest mean accuracy in 24 of 25 controlled settings.
